chapter: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
title: The Town Hall tenor battle and ending the concerts
summary: He holds a sold-out tenor battle with Lester Young, gives away his profits, and stops the series in 1947.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: So then I continued to have these festivals, these sessions in the foyer. And then I decided to have a battle of the tenor saxophones, at Town Hall with Lester Young and Zack something and Jimmy Oliver. Was Jimmy Oliver a tenor saxophone player? You remember that name?
And I'm telling you, on a Sunday...this was on Sunday...at Town Hall in Philadelphia. I came up in a cab and I saw all of these people coming up out of the subway, in cars and

and that and this, and I said, "What on earth is happening? Maybe they had an accident or something." And I got in that Town Hall in Philadelphia and it was packed to the rafters. And we had a very, very successful concert.

But my only problem, Dan, was I had no conception about money. If our net profit was three hundred dollars after we'd paid everybody and all expenses taken/ I'd take the three hundred dollars and entertain the musicians with it. You know, take them to a restaurant and have chicken and food and that and this, and, you know. And I never...I never really made a profit out of those concerts. But I had these concerts until '47 and then I discontinued them because there was a guy in Philadelphia that had a club...he started having, you know, jazz every night, you know, and all. And then sometimes some of the musicians didn't show up and this would creat a problem. He'd advertise, you know, a group of people and then if somebody don't show up the guy says you're lying. He didn't want to accept the fact that perhaps the guy...and all it was is the guy just got a better job, you know.
